IGCSE Physics - Chapter 10: Electricity & Electronics (1-8)

Question 1

(0625/42_Summer_2017_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 8.1 shows a 12.0V power supply connected in a circuit.

The circuit includes a lamp and a resistance wire AB of constant cross-sectional area. There is a sliding contact that can be moved between A and B.

(a) The rating of the lamp at normal brightness is 6.0V, 9.0W.

Calculate

(i) the current in the lamp at normal brightness, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using the formula P = V × I, we can find the current I.

I = P⁄V = 9.0 W⁄6.0 V = 1.5 A

(ii) the resistance of the lamp at normal brightness. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using Ohm's Law, V = I × R, we can find the resistance R.

R = V⁄I = 6.0 V⁄1.5 A = 4.0 Ω

(b) AB is 1.00 m long and has a resistance of 5.0Ω. The lamp has normal brightness when the sliding contact is at X.

(i) The sliding contact is moved to B. Explain, without a calculation, why the lamp becomes dimmer. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

When the contact is moved to B, the length of the resistance wire in the circuit increases. This increases the total resistance of the circuit. A higher total resistance leads to a lower current flowing through the lamp, and a smaller p.d. across the lamp, making it dimmer.

(ii) Calculate the distance AX for the lamp to have normal brightness. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

For normal brightness, current is 1.5 A. The total resistance of the circuit is Rtotal = Vsupply⁄I = 12.0 V⁄1.5 A = 8.0 Ω.

The total resistance is the sum of the lamp's resistance and the resistance of the wire section AX. Rtotal = Rlamp + RAX.

So, RAX = 8.0 Ω - 4.0 Ω = 4.0 Ω.

The wire's resistance is proportional to its length. The full length (1.00 m) has 5.0 Ω. The distance AX is (4.0 Ω⁄5.0 Ω) × 1.00 m = 0.80 m.

Question 2

(0625/41_Summer_2017_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

(a) The resistance of a circuit component varies with the brightness of the light falling on its surface.

(i) State the name of the component. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The component is a Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR).

(ii) Draw the circuit symbol for this component. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows a 6.0V battery connected in series with a 1.2kΩ resistor and a thermistor.

(i) At a certain temperature, the resistance of the thermistor is 2.4 kΩ. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

The total resistance in the series circuit is 1.2 kΩ + 2.4 kΩ = 3.6 kΩ.

The voltmeter reading is the potential difference across the thermistor. Using the potential divider formula:

Vout = Vin × (Rthermistor⁄Rtotal)

Vout = 6.0 V × (2.4 kΩ⁄3.6 kΩ) = 4.0 V.

(ii) The battery connected to the circuit in Fig. 9.1 is not changed. Suggest a change that would cause the reading of the voltmeter to decrease. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

To decrease the voltmeter reading (p.d. across the thermistor), the thermistor's resistance must decrease relative to the fixed resistor. This can be achieved by increasing the temperature of the thermistor.

Question 3

(0625/43_Summer_2017_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

A 12V battery is connected in series to a 24W lamp and to a parallel pair of identical resistors X and Y. Fig. 9.1 is the circuit diagram.

The 24 W lamp lights at normal brightness when the potential difference (p.d.) across it is 6.0V. The lamp is at normal brightness.

(a) Calculate the resistance of the lamp. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

First, find the current at normal brightness: I = P⁄V = 24 W⁄6.0 V = 4.0 A.

Then, calculate resistance: R = V⁄I = 6.0 V⁄4.0 A = 1.5 Ω.

(b) Determine

(i) the p.d. between A and B, [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The p.d. across the parallel pair is the supply voltage minus the p.d. across the lamp: 12 V - 6.0 V = 6.0 V.

(ii) the combined resistance of the parallel pair of identical resistors X and Y, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The current through the parallel pair is the same as the current through the lamp, 4.0 A. The combined resistance is Rcombined = VAB⁄I = 6.0 V⁄4.0 A = 1.5 Ω.

(iii) the resistance of X. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

For two identical resistors in parallel, Rcombined = RX⁄2.

Therefore, RX = 2 × Rcombined = 2 × 1.5 Ω = 3.0 Ω.

(c) Resistor X is removed from the circuit in Fig 9.1. Explain why the lamp becomes dimmer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

When resistor X is removed, the total resistance of the parallel part of the circuit increases (from 1.5 Ω to 3.0 Ω). This increases the total resistance of the entire circuit. As a result, the total current decreases, causing the lamp to become dimmer.

Question 7

(0625/42_Summer_2018_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 8.1 shows a circuit that contains a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 6.0V, an ammeter, a 20Ω resistor and component X.

(a) (i) State the name of component X. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Component X is a variable resistor or rheostat.

(ii) The potential difference (p.d.) across the 20Ω resistor is measured with a voltmeter. On Fig. 8.1, draw the symbol for this voltmeter connected to the circuit. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(b) The p.d. across the 20Ω resistor is varied from zero to 6.0V. For each value of p.d. a corresponding current is measured.

On Fig. 8.2, draw a line to indicate how the current measured by the ammeter depends on the p.d. across the 20Ω resistor. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Since the resistor is ohmic, the graph is a straight line through the origin. The maximum current is I = V⁄R = 6.0 V⁄20 Ω = 0.30 A. The line should be a straight line from (0, 0) to (6.0 V, 0.30 A).

(c) A second resistor is connected into the circuit in parallel with the 20Ω resistor.

(i) State how the combined resistance of the two resistors in parallel compares with the resistance of each of the resistors on its own. [1]

The combined resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

(ii) The p.d. across the two parallel resistors is changed and the current in the battery for each value of the p.d. is measured. A second line could be drawn on Fig. 8.2 to indicate how the current measured by the ammeter depends on the p.d. across the two resistors in parallel. State how the second line differs from the original line. You are not expected to draw this second line. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Because the combined resistance is lower, for the same p.d. the current will be higher. Therefore, the second line would be steeper (have a greater gradient) than the original line.

Question 8

Tap to reveal answer

1. Bring the positively charged rod close to, but not touching, the conducting sphere.

2. Earth the sphere by touching it with your finger. Electrons will be attracted from the earth onto the sphere.

3. Remove the earth connection (your finger) while the rod is still held close.

4. Finally, remove the rod. The sphere will be left with a net negative charge.

Question 10

(0625/42_Winter_2019_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

(a) A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 0.40 mm2 has a resistance of 0.14Ω. Calculate the resistance of another wire of the same material of length 3.0m and cross-sectional area 0.90 mm2. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Resistance (R) is directly proportional to length (L) and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (A).

R ∝ L⁄A

R2 = R1 × (L2⁄L1) × (A1⁄A2)

R2 = 0.14 Ω × (3.0 m⁄2.0 m) × (0.40 mm2⁄0.90 mm2)

R2 = 0.14 × 1.5 × 0.444... = 0.093 Ω

Question 11

(0625/43_Winter_2019_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit containing an LED and two resistors in parallel, each of resistance R.

The normal operating voltage of the LED is 2.1 V and the normal current is 0.19A.

(a) (i) The potential difference (p.d.) across the LED is measured with a voltmeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this voltmeter connected to the circuit. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(ii) The current in the LED is measured with an ammeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this ammeter connected to the circuit. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(b) Calculate the value of R when the LED is operating normally. [5]

Tap to reveal answer

The p.d. across the parallel resistors is VR = Vsupply - VLED = 3.7 V - 2.1 V = 1.6 V.

The total current flowing through the parallel combination is the same as the current through the LED, which is 0.19 A.

The combined resistance of the two parallel resistors is Rparallel = VR⁄Itotal = 1.6 V⁄0.19 A ≈ 8.42 Ω.

For two identical resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is Rparallel = R⁄2.

Therefore, R = 2 × Rparallel = 2 × 8.42 Ω ≈ 16.84 Ω.

So, R is approximately 17 Ω.

Question 12

(0625/41_Summer_2020_Q9) - Electron And Electronics

(a) Describe how a digital signal differs from an analogue signal. You may draw a diagram. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A digital signal consists of only two discrete states or values, often represented as high and low, or 1 and 0. An analogue signal is continuously varying and can have any value within a given range.

(b) (i) In the appropriate box, draw the symbol for an AND gate and the symbol for an OR gate. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(ii) State how the behaviour of an AND gate differs from that of an OR gate. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

An AND gate produces a high output (1) only if all of its inputs are high. An OR gate produces a high output if at least one of its inputs is high.

(c) An arrangement of logic gates A, B and C is shown in Fig. 9.1. The arrangement has two inputs, X and Y and two outputs P and Q.

Output P of logic gate B has logic state 1 (high).

(i) Determine the logic states of the two inputs of logic gate B. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Gate B is a NOR gate. For a NOR gate to have an output of 1, both of its inputs must be 0.

upper input = 0, lower input = 0.

(ii) Determine and explain the logic state of output Q. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

State of Q = 0. Explanation: The lower input to gate B is Y, so Y must be 0. The upper input to B is the output of gate A (a NAND gate). For gate A's output to be 0, both its inputs must be 1. One input to A is X, so X must be 1. The other input to A is also X, which is consistent. Gate C is a NOR gate. Its inputs are X (1) and Y (0). With inputs of 1 and 0, a NOR gate gives an output Q of 0.

Question 15

(0625/42_Winter_2020_Q10) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 10.1 shows an incomplete electrical circuit.

(a) (i) A student completes the circuit and measures the current in the 6.0Ω resistor. On Fig. 10.1, draw an ammeter symbol in one gap and straight lines to indicate wires in the other gaps to show how the student should do this. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(ii) A voltmeter is connected to measure the potential difference (p.d.) across the 4.0Ω resistor. On Fig. 10.1, draw a voltmeter symbol connected in the correct position. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

(iii) With the circuit completed, the current in the 2.0Ω resistor is 2.5A. Calculate the current in the 6.0Ω resistor. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

The p.d. across the 2.0Ω resistor is V = I × R = 2.5 A × 2.0 Ω = 5.0 V. Since the 4.0Ω resistor is in parallel, the p.d. across it is also 5.0 V. The current in the 4.0Ω resistor is I = V⁄R = 5.0 V⁄4.0 Ω = 1.25 A.

The total current leaving the parallel combination is the current in the 6.0Ω resistor: 2.5 A + 1.25 A = 3.75 A (or 3.8 A).

Question 16

(0625/43_Winter_2020_Q10) - Electron And Electronics

Fig. 10.1 shows a relay.

(a) The switch in circuit A is closed. Describe how this operates the motor in circuit B. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

When the switch in circuit A is closed, current flows through the coil, turning the soft-iron core into a magnet. This electromagnet attracts the iron armature. The armature pivots and pushes the contacts together, completing circuit B and operating the motor.

(b) The switch in circuit A is opened. The soft-iron armature is replaced with a steel armature. The switch in circuit A is closed. Explain what happens when the switch in circuit A is then opened. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

When the switch is opened, the current in the coil stops, but because the core is now steel, it remains magnetised (it becomes a permanent magnet). Therefore, it continues to hold the armature, and the motor in circuit B does not stop.

Question 17

(0625/41_Summer_2021_Q8) - Electron And Electronics

A student sets up a circuit that includes a 12V battery, an 800Ω resistor, a voltmeter and a thermistor. Fig. 8.1 is an incomplete circuit diagram because the symbol for the thermistor is missing. The thermistor is connected between terminals P and Q.

(a) Complete Fig. 8.1 by drawing the symbol for a thermistor between terminals P and Q. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(b) The 12V battery consists of eight identical cells connected in series. Calculate the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of each cell. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

e.m.f. per cell = Total e.m.f.⁄Number of cells = 12 V⁄8 = 1.5 V.

(c) The reading on the voltmeter is 8.0V.

(i) Determine the resistance of the thermistor. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The voltmeter measures the p.d. across the thermistor, which is 8.0 V. The p.d. across the 800Ω resistor is 12 V - 8.0 V = 4.0 V.

The current in the circuit is I = V⁄R = 4.0 V⁄800 Ω = 0.0050 A.

The resistance of the thermistor is RTh = VTh⁄I = 8.0 V⁄0.0050 A = 1600 Ω.

(ii) A few hours later, the student notices that the reading on the voltmeter is greater. Explain what can be deduced from this observation. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

A greater voltmeter reading means a larger proportion of the e.m.f. is across the thermistor. This implies that the resistance of the thermistor has increased. For a thermistor, resistance increases when the temperature decreases. Therefore, the room has become cooler.

(c) An electrical device has a metal case. Explain the benefit of earthing the metal case. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Earthing prevents electrocution. If a live wire touches the metal case, the earth wire provides a low resistance path for the current to flow to the ground. This causes a large surge of current that blows the fuse or trips the circuit breaker, disconnecting the supply and making the appliance safe.

(d) (i) Explain how a fuse protects a circuit. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A fuse contains a thin wire designed to melt at a specific current. If the current becomes too high due to a fault, the wire heats up and melts. This breaks the circuit and stops the flow of current, protecting the appliance from damage.

(ii) The current in an electric kettle connected to the mains through a fuse is 10A. Fuses with the following ratings are available. Circle the correct fuse rating for this appliance and explain your answer. 3A 9A 10A 13A 30A

Tap to reveal answer

Correct fuse rating: 13 A.

Explanation: The fuse rating must be slightly higher than the normal operating current. A 10A fuse might blow during normal operation, while 9A and 3A are too low. 30A is too high and would not protect the appliance.

Question 22

(0625/41_Summer_2022_Q9) - Electron And Electronics

(a) Describe the difference between a digital signal and an analogue signal. You may include a diagram if it helps your answer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

A digital signal consists of only two discrete states, 1s and 0s (high and low). An analogue signal is continuously variable in magnitude.

(b) Input A is the output of a humidity sensor which gives logic 1 when the humidity is high and logic 0 when the humidity is low. Input B is the output of a light sensor which gives logic 1 in bright light and logic 0 in darkness. The buzzer sounds when the output of Y is logic 1. State the conditions of humidity and light when the buzzer is on. [1]

(c) The output of the digital circuit alone is not able to operate the buzzer. Ring the component from the list that must be connected between the output of the digital circuit and the buzzer. fuse heater relay resistor thermistor. Explain your answer. [3]

Question 24

(0625/41_Winter_2022_Q9) - Electron And Electronics

Only one isotope of gold occurs naturally on Earth.

(a) State what this indicates about the nuclear structure of all the naturally occurring atoms of gold on Earth. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

This indicates that all naturally occurring gold atoms have the same number of neutrons (as well as the same number of protons).

(b) There are several artificially produced isotopes of gold. Gold-198 decays by beta-emission to a stable isotope of mercury.

(i) Determine the number of protons and the number of neutrons in a nucleus of this isotope of mercury. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Gold-198 is 19879Au. In beta decay, a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted. The proton number increases by 1, and the nucleon number is unchanged.

Number of protons = 79 + 1 = 80.

Number of neutrons = 198 - 80 = 118.

(ii) A sample of gold-198 is placed near to a radiation detector in a research laboratory. The count rate is recorded at the same time every day for 32 days. The results are used to plot the graph shown in Fig. 9.1. Using Fig. 9.1, determine the background count rate in the research laboratory. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The background count rate is the reading after the source has fully decayed. From the graph, the count rate flattens out at 20 counts/min.

(iii) Using Fig. 9.1, determine the half-life of gold-198. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Initial count rate from the source = Initial total count - background count = 390 - 20 = 370 counts/min.

Half of this count rate is 370 / 2 = 185 counts/min.

The total count rate on the graph to look for is 185 + background = 185 + 20 = 205 counts/min.

From the graph, a count rate of 205 counts/min corresponds to a time of approximately 2.7 days. (Accept range 2.4-2.9 days).

Question 25

(0625/42_Winter_2022_Q10) - Electron And Electronics

(a) The magnitude of the charge on a β-particle is 1.6 × 10-19C.

(i) State the proton number and nucleon number of an α-particle. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

proton number: 2

nucleon number: 4

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the charge of an α-particle. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

An α-particle contains 2 protons. The charge is twice the elementary charge.

Charge = 2 × 1.6 × 10-19 C = 3.2 × 10-19 C.

(b) A nucleus of radium-230 consists of 88 protons and 142 neutrons. Radium-230 is radioactive and decays by β-emission to an isotope of actinium. The symbol for radium is Ra and the symbol for actinium is Ac. Write down the nuclide equation for this decay. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

23088Ra → 23089Ac + 0-1β

The nucleon number (230) remains the same on both sides. The proton number on the left (88) equals the sum of the proton numbers on the right (89 + -1).

(c) The half-life of radium-230 is 93 min. A sample contains 9.6 × 10-12g of radium-230. Calculate the mass of radium in the sample after 279 min. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Number of half-lives = Total time⁄Half-life = 279 min⁄93 min = 3.

After 3 half-lives, the mass will have halved three times.

Mass remaining = Initial mass⁄23 = (9.6 × 10-12 g)⁄8 = 1.2 × 10-12 g.

Question 26

(0625/43_Winter_2022_Q10) - Electron And Electronics

(a) A cloud chamber can be used to detect α-particles and β-particles. Alcohol in the cloud chamber exists as a vapour and condenses on ions produced in the air. This forms visible tracks. Fig. 10.1 shows the tracks when a source of α-particles and β-particles is present in the cloud chamber. Some of the tracks are short and thick. Other tracks are longer and thinner. State and explain which tracks are produced by α-particles and which tracks are produced by β-particles. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

α-particles produce the short, thick tracks. This is because they are more ionising, creating a dense trail of ions, but they are less penetrating and have a shorter range.

β-particles produce the long, thin tracks. This is because they are less ionising, creating a sparse trail, but they are more penetrating and have a longer range.

(b) A radioactive isotope of sodium (Na) is used to detect leaks from water pipes. A nucleus of this isotope of sodium contains 11 protons and 13 neutrons. This nucleus decays by emitting a β-particle to form a nucleus of magnesium (Mg).

(i) Describe what is meant by an isotope. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons in their nucleus.

(ii) Write down the nuclide equation for the decay of this isotope of sodium to magnesium. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The isotope is Sodium-24 (11 protons + 13 neutrons).

2411Na → 2412Mg + 0-1β

The nuclide equation is balanced with Na on the left, and Mg and β on the right with correct proton and nucleon numbers.

(iii) This isotope of sodium has a half-life of 15 hours. The isotope of magnesium is stable and does not undergo radioactive decay. Suggest why these properties of the isotope of sodium and the isotope of magnesium make this isotope of sodium suitable to detect leaks from water pipes. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The half-life is long enough to allow time for the leak to be detected. However, it is also short enough that the radioactivity will decay to a negligible amount after a few days, making the water safe. Also, the decay product (magnesium) is stable, so it is not hazardous.
